blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we meet two awesome record-breakers: a jigsaw puzzle with more than half a million pieces, and a little animal that can regrow its own leg.
Ready?
Let's go!
In a big stadium in Vietnam, 1,600 students worked together on the biggest jigsaw puzzle ever made.
It had 551,232 pieces!
When it was finished, the picture was a beautiful lotus flower, nearly 15 meters wide and 23 meters long — bigger than a classroom, bigger than a house!
The puzzle was so big that nobody could work on it all at once.
It was cut into 3,132 small sections, and each team worked on one section.
Each piece had only one valid place.
A piece in the wrong place, and the picture would not work.
With patience and teamwork, the students fitted section after section together.
After 17 hours of work, the last piece clicked into place.
Imagine the cheers!
Even the biggest puzzle you can buy in a shop is much smaller: a puzzle with 54,000 pieces, showing more than 50 famous paintings.
That is still awesome, but the stadium puzzle is ten times bigger.
People enjoy puzzles because every piece is a small mystery.
So remember: no puzzle is too big if you cut it into small parts and work together.
Meet the axolotl, a salamander from Mexico.
In Chinese it is called the "six-horned dinosaur", because of the six feathery gills on its head.
But it is not a dinosaur at all — it is a salamander that keeps its baby looks as a grown-up and lives in the water all its life.
Its delicate, bright pink gills wave in the water like tiny feathers.
Here is the difference between us and the axolotl.
When we get a bad cut, our body makes a scar.
When an axolotl loses a leg, its body does something amazing: it grows a brand-new leg, with new bones, muscles, and even the same skin patterns.
It can do this again and again.
It can also regrow parts of its heart and its spinal cord!
How does it work?
When a leg is lost, the cells under the skin are exposed.
Instead of making a scar, those cells change back into young, growing cells and form a soft lump called a blastema.
The blastema is like a builder's workshop: it slowly builds the missing leg, piece by piece.
Scientists study the axolotl to learn how it recovers so perfectly.
One day, this knowledge might help doctors help people recover from injuries.
In the wild, axolotls live only in the lakes near Mexico City, and they are in danger because their lakes are shrinking.
Scientists are working hard to protect them.
Here's today's idiom: 'bite the bullet.' When you bite the bullet, you do something difficult or unpleasant — you just face it bravely!
Here's an example: 'Tom lost the instructions for his puzzle, but he bit the bullet and started with the edge pieces.' When did you last bite the bullet?
Let's think about our stories: a puzzle with 551,232 pieces, and an animal that can regrow a leg.
First: if you had to bite the bullet and finish a giant puzzle, would you start with the edges, or with your favorite color?
Second: if you could regrow anything, like the axolotl, what would you choose?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Be patient like a puzzler, brave like an axolotl — and when something feels hard, just bite the bullet!
See you tomorrow!
